value: Could be a fun one to use a packraft on, as walking all around the perimeter is a little tricky
July 2026 - Dilworth caught a nice 18 inch brookie here. It was delicious. :)

2020 - magical couple of days here partway through our re-routed Highline attempt, with Dilworth and Hui.

2024 - Dilworth and Ryan and I had repeated success with cutthroats in that little outlet pond, and I caught a few from my packraft out in the middle.

The only report I could find on this, from 2012: https://backcountrypost.com/threads/east-slide-lake-uintas-6-28-12.1019 "The initial part of the Lake Fork trail is not that difficult to traverse. Other than the occasional fallen tree across the path, the trail is pretty well groomed and only rises about 1000ft over the 1st eight miles. Not a lot of boggy areas either (maybe that’s just the dry year?). The last mile and a half to reach East Slide Lake is the tricky part. My original plan was to hike to the confluence of the Oweep and Lake Fork Rivers, follow the Oweep River briefly, and then climb the relatively steep slope to the lake. I thought it was a little strange when I passed a couple of rock cairns about ¾ of a mile from the confluence without any obvious trail branching off. I’m used to cairns marking spur trails, but I knew of no other trails that were supposed to branch off in this location. So I just kept hiking. I knew from the topo maps that the area where the rivers came together had some steep slopes, but I was sure there was probably an area to drop into and out of the river gorge without too much difficulty… nope. At the confluence, the gorge was basically 60-100ft cliffs on either side. No way across here. It was then that I realized that the cairns probably marked the most suitable gorge crossing. So I backtracked, and sure enough just after the cairns there were a couple of areas (although still pretty steep) where one could traverse the gorge safely. […] After starting the day just before 7am, I arrived back at the trailhead around 6:30pm. I would have much preferred to stay overnight so I could have also visited the relatively nearby Gates Lake."

August 2026- Brutal approach! Ryan and I ascended from south at an attempted diagonal, then descended almost straight down the outlet ravine, other than circumnavigating some cliffs near the top. See CalTopo for deets.
Rough road, but quick hike and nice access to many other surrounding lakes.

Sep 2026: Ryan and I took his new truck up the Norway flats Road and parked where 035 branches off to 916, which took 45 minutes. I think his truck would’ve easily made it to where 035 branches 035A. But it was actually a blast ride mountain bikes to the trailhead (15 minutes). We each caught 3 brookies, and surprisingly zero tigers given the stocking record for the last 10 years. Battling the wind in my pack raft wasn’t much fun.

Pretty little lake, and not far off the trail. Could make for some nice camping at times in an area where it’d otherwise be crowded at Island. Trail between Big Elk and Island had tons of nice cairns to link the obvious trail spots together.
Sep 2026 Ryan and I each caught a few small guys.
Sep 2026 - Didn’t have much time. Had one on that broke off. Worked out well to shortcut off trail to the west and link up with the trail back to Big Elk, instead of going back to Island.
Sep 2026- only a few casts, didn’t leave ourselves enough time.
Decent possible campsite on south side
Summer 2025 - Kenny and I thought we were at Start Lake, since we had mistaken a nameless pond to the south for Diamond.
